utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Chester Stamp, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager. And I extend my greetings to the Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence, who aren't all present today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura for today, Mr. Rodney Dixon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present. And the Trial Chamber would like to greet Madam Registrar, who will help us in the course of our work. And I don't want to forget the court reporter or the interpreters either. We have to continue with the hearing of a witness today, but before we do so, the Trial Chamber will render a decision concerning the documents. I have provided the interpreters with a copy of this decision, and please pay careful attention to the decision. The decision relates to the documents. The Trial Chamber hereby renders the following decision: Last Friday the Trial Chamber rendered an oral decision in which it asked the Prosecution to provide the Trial Chamber with a copy of the documents that are contested as soon as possible. The Trial Chamber asked the Defence to provide a written explanation for which they were contesting individual documents, and they were asked to set forth arguments that concern the relevance, the authenticity, and the chain of custody relating to the documents. The Defence was asked to provide by the 8th of April or at a subsequent date, if this was necessary for the Defence, a response to the questions put to it by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber also asked the Prosecutor to respond to the written submissions of the Defence by the 19th of April. The Trial Chamber stated that following the exchanges between the Prosecution and the Defence, the Trial Chamber would hold a particular hearing concerning these documents, and we indicated that these documents would be marked for identification. The Trial Chamber took this decision in order to structure the debate on the admissibility of documents, given the vast amount of documents that are contested by the Defence. There are over 600 such documents. Following this decision rendered on last Friday, the Defence stated yesterday that the explanations that they had been requested to provide would make it necessary for them to draft a document of 2 or 3 hundred pages and that that would require at least six weeks of work. In addition, the Defence stated that it would be difficult for them to set forth their arguments for each document because the Defence claimed that the Prosecution had not yet claimed how they were going to use these documents. The Trial Chamber then demanded that the Defence should state its position on Monday; that is to say, yesterday. The Defence presented its arguments in detail, and the Prosecution responded to the arguments set forth by the Defence. The Trial Chamber would summarise the debate as follows: In the Defence's opinion, they can't be requested to provide detailed explanations regarding the contested documents at this point in time, since such explanations, in the Defence's opinion, should be provided after the Prosecution has finished presenting its case. The Defence pointed out that it was possible to tender documents into evidence without doing so through a witness, but in the Defence's opinion the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the practice of this Tribunal to date is in favour of tendering documents through witnesses. By following this procedure, in the Defence's opinion, the Prosecution could indicate, after it has concluded its case, they could indicate whether they intend to use all the documents that haven't been tendered and they could indicate category by category what the relevance and the source of these documents are. This would then make it possible for the Defence to respond to the arguments set forth by the Prosecution. In the Defence's opinion, the rights of the accused would be better protected in such a case because it would be possible for the Defence to cross-examine witnesses through which documents would be tendered, and thus the burden of proof would still be placed on the Prosecution. The Defence pointed out that only 222 documents are referred to in the pre-trial brief, and the Prosecution provided indications as to how 127 documents would be used, 127 documents which were contested, and this is one of the reasons for which it would be very difficult for the Defence to express its position and, naturally, to set forth its arguments concerning the vast majority of the documents. Following the arguments presented by the Defence, the Prosecution stated the following yesterday - and the Trial Chamber would like to remind you of the arguments presented: Tendering documents directly into evidence, without having recourse to a witness, is a well-established practice. The two main reasons that the Defence presented for contesting documents, in the Prosecution's opinion, are relevance and authenticity. The Prosecution stated that the Defence also identified 12 other factors that affected these two criteria. According to the Prosecution, the Defence did not indicate which of these criteria would be applicable to each document. The Prosecution also stated that the majority of the contested documents came from the Sarajevo archives and that among these documents there were many documents that came from the BH 3rd Corps or from the 7th Brigade. They also stated that about 100 or 50 documents were signed either by one or the other of the accused. If the Defence contests these documents for reasons of authenticity, it is the opinion of the Prosecution that it would be useful to know as soon as possible whether this is the case because resolving this question, in the opinion of the Prosecution, might require an expert evaluation of the signatures on the documents. We believe that the burden of proof has not been reversed, because the Prosecution still has to demonstrate to the Trial Chamber that the documents are relevant and authentic. Following the observations made by the Defence and by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber on this day sees no reason to reconsider the decision it rendered last Friday. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that it would be in the interest of justice to clarify its decision and to add certain other elements to it. On the basis of the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence governing this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber has to ensure that the proceedings are expeditious and that the proceedings are fair with respect to both parties, and naturally, it is necessary for the rights of both accused to be respected. The Trial Chamber must ensure that the evidence is efficiently Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. presented for the sake of determining the truth, and at the same time it is necessary to avoid wasting time. This is the Trial Chamber's obligation pursuant to Rule 92(F) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Trial Chamber would also like to state that according to Rule 65 ter of the Rules concerning the pre-trial stage of the proceedings provides, and I quote, "The Prosecutor must on each occasion state whether the Defence contests or not the authenticity of exhibits." As a result, it is the Trial Chamber's opinion that the Defence should be requested to set forth the grounds for which it is contesting the documents presented by the Prosecution. These are documents that they have had in their possession for a number of months now. The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the burden of proof has not been reversed, given that pursuant to Rule 89 it is still for the Prosecution to convince the Trial Chamber that a document should be admitted into evidence, and they should do this by demonstrating the relevance and authenticity of the documents concerned. Naturally the Defence is not requested to provide proof that the Prosecution's documents should not be admitted into evidence. The Trial Chamber is not of the opinion that a document can be admitted into evidence for the sole reason that it has not been sufficiently contested by the Defence. The Defence is simply requested to state its position with regard to a given document. The Prosecution has to demonstrate that there is no reason for not admitting a document into evidence. As a result, the Trial Chamber - and please pay careful attention to what I'm going to say now - as a result, the Trial Chamber orders that the Defence submit a written document to the Trial Chamber by the 19th -- on the 19th of April, 2004. First of all, the contested documents should be placed into categories, and the reasons for which they are being contested should be set forth, reasons such as relevance, authenticity, and also the 12 other factors mentioned that may affect these two criteria. The Defence should state in one or two lines the reasons for which they are contesting each document. And thirdly - this is important; please pay attention - the Defence should indicate which documents in their opinion can only be tendered into evidence through a witness. And they should also indicate in which cases it's absolutely necessary to cross-examine a witness. So I'll summarise what I have just said. The Defence has three obligations to comply with: Firstly, with regard to the 600-odd documents that are contested, the Defence has to set forth the categories that these documents belong to. These categories could be based on relevance or authenticity or on the 12 factors that you have mentioned. In addition, to respond to your argument concerning the 300 pages, we are only requesting that you write one line for each document, so that won't amount to 300 pages. Thirdly, you should inform us -- with regard to the 655 documents, you should inform us which documents are absolutely necessary and which documents can only be tendered into evidence through a witness. So these are the three points that I wanted to indicate with regard to the Defence. As far as the Prosecution is concerned - and I can see that Mr. Withopf has a pen in his hands. He will pay careful attention to his obligations - the Trial Chamber requests that the Prosecution present to the Trial Chamber a written submission by the 19th of April. In this submission, the Prosecution should indicate on the basis of the categories concerning the documents, they should indicate the source and information concerning the chain of custody. Secondly, the Prosecution should provide the Trial Chamber with more detailed information about the source or the origin of the listed documents, if they are from unknown sources, because in the consolidated list there are documents for which no source has been indicated. The Trial Chamber would like to know what the origin and source of these documents are. So the Prosecution should indicate the source of these documents when the source hasn't been indicated. Thirdly, the Prosecution should indicate to the Trial Chamber the reason for which the transcripts of testimony of witnesses in other cases before the Tribunal are included in the list of the Prosecution's exhibits, and it -- they haven't followed the procedure pursuant to Rule 92 bis(D) and (E). And fourthly, the Prosecution is requested to indicate in rough terms what the relevance of the documents that haven't been referred to in the pre-trial brief is, documents which have not yet been admitted. Because we note that there are several hundred documents that aren't referred to in the pre-trial brief, so we would like some information from the Prosecution about this matter. Having received written submissions from the Defence and the Prosecution, it is the intention of the Trial Chamber to have a hearing in order to discuss the subject of the admissibility of documents into evidence. This particular hearing relating to these documents could be held either one week before the expert witness General Reinhardt is heard or one week after his hearing. The written submissions provided by the parties, as we have mentioned, before this hearing would make it possible to structure the debate and to proceed in a more efficient manner, and it would allow the Trial Chamber and the parties to prepare themselves in an appropriate manner. As a result, the hearings would be structured. This would be done by following the most logical categories in the light of the written submissions of the parties. And during these hearings, the duration of which will be determined after having taken note of the written submissions, these hearings will last for a number of days, for one week at a minimum. In the course of these hearings, the Prosecution, in order to avoid wasting any time, the Prosecution will indicate document by document the reasons for which documents in a given category should be admitted. The Defence will then be requested to make a response and to set forth its arguments relating to the Prosecution's arguments. So this is our decision. Please reread the transcript carefully. Both parties should inform us about the request by the 19th of April. There are three points for the Defence and four points that the Prosecution has to address. This will make it possible for us to advance with the examination of these documents in a more efficient manner. And as you have understood, we believe that it is necessary to have a hearing dedicated to the discussion of these documents. In order to be able to hold this hearing, we need to know what the categories of documents are. So both parties are requested to provide us with this information. Naturally, if you are not in a position to do this, the Trial Chamber will do this. But as the parties make the proceedings advance, this is your obligation. But if you are not in a position to do so, the Trial Chamber will intervene. It is for the parties to tell us what the categories of documents are. Naturally we aren't requesting that you draft 300 pages. We only ask that you write one line for each document. So that should be sufficient time -- you should have sufficient time by the 19th of April. We will then have a hearing and we will discuss each individual document. So there are two possibilities: Either we will have this hearing one week before General Reinhardt is heard, or one week after. Naturally, the Prosecution is in charge of scheduling witnesses. It is for them to see when this might be possible. But roughly speaking, one week should be quite sufficient. Please reread the decision very carefully, and we will then follow it. We'll now ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom, because as you know, we have to have a break between 5.00 and 6.00. We will resume at 6.00, and I have asked the legal officer to see with the registry and the other relevant services whether we could continue after this hour in order to finish hearing the witness. As we have already said, the Trial Chamber also has some questions that it would like to put Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the witness. Regarding the witness, the hearing will be resumed by the re-examination by the Prosecution, who asked to have overnight to prepare their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But we need to wait for the witness to arrive, Mr. Stamp. I know you don't want to waste any time, but let's wait for the witness to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sit down, please. The Chamber greets you and thanks you for staying overnight to be able to answer additional questions that will be put to you by Mr. Stamp, who represents the Prosecutor. Mr. Stamp, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Zeric.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said yesterday in answering a question put by my friend for the Defence that there was a basic prosecutor's office in Travnik as well as a basic prosecutor's office in Bugojno. Just for clarification, if there were reports of offences committed by ABiH or Bosnian government army personnel in Bugojno, would those reports go to your office?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a report was filed against a member of the army, every prosecutor's office is obliged to pass on the case to the competent prosecutor's office. And if it feels that it is not within a jurisdiction, it would pass it on to another prosecutor's office. So if it was filed with the basic prosecutor's office in Travnik or Bugojno and if they were army personnel, it was their obligation to pass on that case to us for further processing, and vice versa. If it was a question of civilians, we would pass on the case to the basic prosecutor's office in Travnik or Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Which brings me - and that's a very good segue - to another answer that you gave in respect to civilians. You said that when there was a mixture of civilian and military personnel accused of having committed an offence, according -- or in accordance with Article 9 of the -- I forgot my glasses, but it -- Article 9 in respect to district military courts. The civilian court in Travnik would have responsibility where there was an admixture of civilian and military accused. You said that. Can you elaborate upon that a little bit further?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If a crime was committed by two persons as co-perpetrators, or several persons some of whom were military and others civilian, in that case according to the provisions of that decree which was in force, had the force of law, the case would be dealt with by regular civilian courts or prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were presented with quite a few documents, which I don't propose to review or have you review unless you really need to see one. The documents that you were shown, in particular those reports that you made, indicate that you operated under very difficult conditions, particularly lack of funding. That is so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Notwithstanding those difficulties, yourself and other members of your office, as indeed the court, the military court quite laudably continued to function effectively during the period 1993 to 1996. Would you agree that that is evident from those reports that you sent?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. We did carry out our basic tasks and duties. I have to emphasise that at the time in the prosecutor's office of which I was in charge there were two deputies in addition to myself and two administrative clerks. The whole body consisted of five staff members. And as you were able to see, there were years when we had up to a thousand cases. But in most cases, we worked well in view of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed you said at page 44 -- well, you said yesterday - you wouldn't really know the page number in the transcript - that -- actually, it's not even page 44. You said yesterday, though, that the court and the staff members sometimes went as far as to investigate crimes in the vicinity of the confrontation lines. That is how seriously you took your tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My friend mentioned page 44. I don't see that line. Maybe the pagination is not the same, because there's the official and non-official version. I would just like to know where we are, on what page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stamp, you mentioned page 44. Are you sure of the page, or is it according to your memory? Because Mr. Bourgon, who doesn't need glasses, can't find it on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As the today's transcript reveals at page 13, I did say immediately that it's not page 44, as a matter of fact. Indeed, it's page 55 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 55, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 55 and 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "although in a larger number of cases we actually had to go into the field, where we instigated investigations. For example, Bugojno and Vitez, we investigated investigations in the immediate vicinity of the front lines." That surely that is an indication of how you took your responsibility seriously. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did investigate. And there were even trials sometimes, if conditions permitted, if we had the minimum technical requirements for a trial. In view of the shortage of means of transport and everything else, we actually had to go towards the suspects and the accused, instead of them coming to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you were presented yesterday with a few batches of documents involving reports made by various military police departments, requests for investigations that your office made, and even judgements by the court itself. And I perused most of them; almost all of them related to crimes against property, like theft. Did you see any of them related to crimes involving the burning of Croat houses by ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown yesterday one such document, when a person in addition to theft also burnt a Croat house. I even remember the name, Mujicic Serif [phoen]. I remember that event. And this offence at the time was qualified as one of the graver offences, and that person, as far as I remember, was held in detention for quite some time, and he was sentenced to a higher term. I think that at the time and even pursuant to current laws any burning of facilities or provoking a general danger is qualified as an offence of general danger, a threat to property or a threat to body and limb of other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My real concern was the number of such reports among the batches you saw. You said you saw just one such Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday. Yesterday I saw one. But in relation to the general situation? Is that what you're referring to? You mean in relation to all the reports I received?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. You did, in answer to me, say yesterday - and I'll just quote it - and this is at page 36: "Q. Can you recall if you received any reports from ABiH military units about ABiH soldiers being involved in burning Croat homes? And your answer was: "A. I never received such reports." And that is what -- that is not exactly what I'm asking you now. I'm really asking you about the documents. Basically the document that you were shown by the Defence yesterday related only in one instance to the burning of a Croat house. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that. And I think that reports of that kind and documents of that kind were very rare. And I didn't recall them when you asked me the question, and it was only when I saw the document that I remembered the event, because this was a long time ago, and that those reports with such offences were very, very rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely what I wanted to clarify. However, among the batch of documents that you received from the Defence or you were shown by the Defence yesterday - and that is all I'm asking you about now, those documents that you were shown by the Defence yesterday - you didn't see any relevant to the killing of Croats who were detained in any prison or detention facility, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You didn't see any documents among those batches that related to the killing of Croats on any of the following dates, the 26th of January, 1993, the 24th of April, 1993, and the 8th of June, 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't pay attention to the dates, but I think that there weren't any detained civilians killed by members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of course being a prosecutor yourself you would go by reports you received; well, withdrawn. That is an argument, not so much of a question. You didn't among the batch of documents you received yesterday see any of them in relation to the damaging of Croat Roman Catholic churches or monasteries, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I didn't review all those documents in detail, but just leafing through them superficially I don't think I did notice any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Neither among those documents that you were shown, you didn't see any relevant to any Croat prisoner who was severely beaten or mistreated in any detention facility, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't, except that one woman -- no, I don't think I did see any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Interestingly, some of the documents you were shown - and just for the record and the Court I am speaking primarily but not exclusively to the batch of documents comprising D121 - involved reports that were made by various officials from ABiH military police to your office, and some of these reports involved or included among them statements taken from witnesses by these military police units. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Some of these reports even included references to offences committed by persons who were unidentified. Do you recall seeing some of those yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were reports against unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct in understanding, then, that the military police were not only expected and duty-bound to simply make a report to you but it was a practice, perhaps even their duty, to also do some form of preliminary investigation, perhaps even just taking a statement, before a report was made? Is that conclusion a reasonable and fair one, having regard to those documents that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, it was the duty of the police to collect a minimum of evidence and to attach them to the criminal report, because just to file a criminal report wouldn't mean anything for us. So they were obliged to take those statements. But we didn't use those statements after that. This was just a basis for the criminal proceedings to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Which means, if I could take it a step further - and tell me if you agree with this - that should a commander receive information that persons, many persons have been murdered or killed, or that many persons held in detention have been severely beaten, it would be the responsibility of the commander to at least instigate a preliminary investigation of those allegations.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having learnt of any offence being committed, it is normal for the person - and that is the military police, the security organs - should undertake the steps proscribed by the law, and that means first of all to try and discover the perpetrator so that we as the judicial body could continue our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And certainly, in respect to serious offences like murder, especially mass murder or murder of more than one person, your office could receive, if a commander was, interested, a report, even if the perpetrators were not precisely identified.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice. The prosecutor's office would receive a report even if persons were not identified, with a description of the event and the basic elements that the police collected about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So just to wrap up on this section, the basic responsibility of the commander is not only to report these offences to you, as you indicated in your evidence in chief, but also to start some type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm quite sure it's harmless, but since I don't speak the language, I don't think it should be -- counsel should speak so loudly that, you know, I could hear from across here. I'm quite sure, you know, it's nothing really for the witness, but just as a matter of appearances one should be careful. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, having gone to investigate offences reported in the facility of the front lines -- withdrawn. Had you received reports in respect to murders and savage beatings of prisoners and had you therefore investigated, would you agree that those reports might have, assuming that these things were happening, prevented the continuation of these offences?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to ask the witness to make conclusions of this kind and express an opinion of this kind I feel is absolutely inappropriate. This is a fact witness who has provided all the relevant facts, and I think it is absolutely inappropriate to ask the witness to comment on conclusions that are being offered to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, without making any conclusions, the questions put by Mr. Stamp are quite precise. In view of your position as a military prosecutor, did you have any knowledge of murder committed of persons who were detained by soldiers of the BiH army? So we are not asking you an opinion. Do you have any knowledge of this type of event or not? It's a very precise question. Perhaps the question could be a bit confusing, which explains the opposition of the Defence, but by rephrasing the question, as I am doing, that is: As a military prosecutor, did you have any knowledge of events linked to murder, murder of victims by BiH soldiers? It's a very precise question, a technical question, and it's being addressed to a professional. So what would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered a similar question already yesterday. I think that during the war and while I was the district military prosecutor, I had not heard of the murder or torture of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. civilians by members of the BiH army. Because if I had heard about them, it would have been my official duty to instigate proceedings, regardless of whether I had received a report or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So your reply is very precise. Continue, Mr. Stamp. That was the gist of your question, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There is just one last related to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And had you so proceeded to initiate proceedings in respect to these reports, if you had received them, would you expect that your initiation of proceedings might have prevented or led to the punishment of some of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I withdraw the question. We will address it another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's withdrawing it, so please sit down, Mr. Bourgon. As far as I am able to understand, the re-examination is over. Has the Defence following the re-examination any additional questions? If not, the Judges have some questions. But only questions related to the replies given to the additional questions of the Prosecution. Do not go beyond that scope, Madam Residovic. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's within the veiling of the court to decide how these proceedings should be conducted, but earlier the court had decided that we would cut it according to the basic Rules: Direct examination, cross-examination, redirect. The counsel seeks a second bite of the cherry, to cross-examine again. And then she might ask questions about the documents which might require another late-night stint on behalf of the Prosecution trying to get to it. I don't think it ought to be allowed. When she indicated that her cross-examination was sufficient, I tried to assist by offering her documents not 6/5:56 whether wanted to put in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Defence is not allowed to ask questions following the re-examination of the Prosecution except if those questions have produced new elements. That's all. That is the law. Madam Residovic, only on questions that were put and that might have led to new elements. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving us an opportunity to ask a few questions in connection with the

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zeric, the Prosecutor asked you some questions regarding reports of burning of houses. You said that there were few such reports to the best of your recollection. Is it true, Mr. Zeric, that out of 1.000 cases that you had to deal with your two deputies shared your work with you on an equal footing?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, each one of us took care of one-third of the load, but it was me who mostly received those criminal reports. I would assign those cases to my deputies and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, Mr. Zeric, that after all you may not remember each and every case that you had in your hands in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to review all those cases to be able to remember, because since then at least 10 to 15 thousand criminal reports have passed through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, I will show you another report of the burning of a house for you to confirm whether this is another one of those that you didn't recollect. And, of course, it is to be found in the archives of the cantonal prosecutor's office, which contain all the 1.000 cases that you processed in 1993. So as not to take too much time, I'll come back to that case. I just want to ask you first whether it is true that the military police and the security bodies of the BH army in accordance with the law had the duty to investigate and report criminal offences committed by members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina only.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Everything else was done by the civilian police and the judicial civilian authorities that existed parallel with the military ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If army authorities were to find out that certain offences might have been committed by persons who were not members of the army, then the obligation to investigate the event fell upon the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was taken over by the civilian police, except it was -- if it happened in the combat zone area. Then the military authorities would investigate and pass on the case to the responsible civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, do you know that the army exerted exceptional efforts to protect the monastery in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that the monastery was protected. It was one of the few facilities that was well protected, as compared to other facilities in the area -- combat area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true, Mr. Zeric, that a criminal report was filed against an unknown person who broke into the church in Travnik and that it was never possible to find out who the perpetrators were, that is, the people who entered the church and damaged it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there was a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator. I think that some furniture was broken and that a cross was damaged. I remember those details now. But I don't think the damage in that Catholic church in Travnik was extensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of your district prosecutor's office, would it be correct to say that there weren't any cases of religious facilities being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, not a single religious or holy building in Travnik and beyond - that is to say, in all the municipalities that we covered - no such building was blown up or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And one last question before I show you this document is: Mr. Zeric, are you aware in 1993 the army that you cooperated with, the organs of security and the military police, they set aside particular units in order to provide protection for religious buildings and for the clergy?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the area of Travnik and beyond, from the very beginning of the war we received reports according to which religious buildings were being protected, because there were individuals who would have destroyed or damaged those buildings. So in fact, most of those buildings were completely preserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the usher to show the witness a document that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Residovic, could you tell us where you got this document from. What is its source?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was found in the archives of the cantonal prosecutor's office in Travnik. The witness in response to a question put to him by the Prosecution told us where the prosecutor's office archives was located, and the Defence examined all the archives of the court and of the prosecutor's office and found this document in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, yesterday you explained the procedure followed by the prosecutor's office. I showed you a number of documents, requests for launching investigations into certain acts that -- for which reports had been filed with you. After your requests, would it be correct to say that courts took decisions about conducting investigations and this in fact amounted to the initiation of criminal proceedings? Is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this one of the decisions taken on the basis of a request submitted by the district military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of our request to the judge, he took a decision on conducting an investigation. And in fact, the person mentioned thus no longer -- was no longer a suspect; he was an accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a request to establish whether abandoned houses had been torched, the houses of local Croats, and this was committed by the accused?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The court took a decision on the basis of this report, that there was a danger posed. I can't tell you exactly what this concerns, that it's a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "In the early morning hours on the 14th of July in a drunken state --" and then you can't see something. It says: "In Travnik he set fire to the abandoned houses of local Croats owned by Ante Janjic [phoen], et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that the witness has identified this document as a document from his prosecutor's office and it was a document adopted -- issued on the basis of a request from his prosecutor's office, could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a document from the court. It was preceded by a document from the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can this be seen in the statement of reasons, where it says that this decision was taken on the basis of a request conducting an investigation from the district prosecutor's office in Travnik? The date is the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You received this court document, and there is a stamp from your prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was forwarded to the military district prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the additional explanations, I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The problem is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- a lot of the original is obliterated. That's the first problem. I don't know if there's a copy -- whether the words of the B/C/S copy are a little bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution has said that the B/C/S document has parts that have been deleted. So was a marker used? Was the intention to conceal some of the sentences? What can the Defence say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've heard about the conditions in which the prosecution and the court in Travnik had to work. A document of this kind is in the archives because the deputy or the judge who worked on this made a note of this in those conditions. But if you use a good pair of glasses, you can see everything in the document. And the document was translated by CLSS, and the translation contains everything contained in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know how counsel could say that it contains everything in the original if she does not have a clear original with all the words here to show us. However, we could receive it provisionally, pending a good and accurate copy. I think the fact that a translation was done by CLSS indicates that somewhere around there is a copy that can be read. So I wouldn't have any objections to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you don't have any objections. Madam Registrar, could we have a number. Could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This would be marked Exhibit DH123 and DH123/E for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Residovic, could you please hurry up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think there might have been a 123 yesterday. Perhaps an inquiry could be made -- D123 -- DH123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar, could you check that. Perhaps it's 124.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You're correct. Thank you for the correction. So it would be DH124, and the English version, DH124/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, did you want to carry on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to clarify something. This will certainly be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. You saw a document here, a part of which had been effaced. In the course of the previous debate, we spoke about technical shortcomings of certain documents. Mr. President, a number of documents that were obtained from the archives have either parts that have been underlined or that have been marked over. We can't see who has highlighted certain documents or who has underlined certain documents. That's why the translation service, when it receives a document, tries to the best of its ability to reproduce the original and to highlight the parts in the translation if they are highlighted in the original. So when we talk about technical shortcomings that certain documents have, we think that this is something that could be a difficulty when trying to assess documents. I just wanted to clarify this matter. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There can only be two explanations: Either the document was underlined by someone with a felt-tip, a colour felt-tip used to highlight certain phrases, or perhaps there was an amnesty or a law which made it possible for persons who had previously been prosecuted -- made it possible for these people to be amnestied. So perhaps the judicial services was required to efface all elements that might identify the person concerned in these documents. In this B/C/S document, the name appears nevertheless in a number of places. So we don't have a precise answer to this question at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you have a look at the bottom of the document to the left, there is a number which comes from the translation service of this Tribunal, and we could obtain the document that they worked on, since they have managed to translate the document. My colleague is quite correct; it's very difficult to translate a document such as the one presented today. But the translation service managed to do so. So we could produce the document that they used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, Mr. Stamp are you requiring that the document be marked for identification, or regardless of the problems you don't raise any objections? Or what does this document actually state? It say that is a judge from the military Tribunal ordered the launching of an investigation into Mr. Razic, who in a drunken state set fire to houses abandoned by Croat owners. That's all it contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no objections to it. It having been translated by the CLSS, I'm quite sure they had a copy that they could read. And I'm quite sure that they gave us a faithful reproduction of what they had. So I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that will remain DH124. Does the Defence have any other questions, Mrs. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Judges have some questions for the witness. I'll now turn to the Judge sitting on my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as prosecutor you had the power to maintain public order and peace in the area under your jurisdiction. When performing your duties, did you have any working meetings with the BH command? Naturally, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1993 -- I can't remember exactly whether it was in 1993 or whether it was at some other time, but we did have working meetings with people from brigades. Above all, this had to do with helping them in their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what were these meetings? What were the purposes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of these meetings was to improve the quality of the material that we were provided with and to take additional measures in order to discover who the perpetrators of certain crimes were. Quite a lot of criminal reports had been filed against unidentified perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have certainly heard about foreign combatants, about the Mujahedin. Did you receive any reports from the BH command that concerned the actions of these foreign combatants, of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we didn't receive any such reports. We didn't receive any criminal reports against such combatants either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: Did you receive any files, any documents from the BH command that concerned war crimes committed by soldiers and violations of the Geneva Conventions and of humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive any such reports. We didn't receive any reports that referred to violations of the Geneva Conventions and violations of the way in which a war should be conducted. I should also add that at that time we used the Geneva Conventions to a very slight extent and almost not at all in the course of performing our law enforcement duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the Judge who is sitting to my left to ask the witness some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I would like to put to you a few questions on your activities as a prosecutor in Bosnia in 1993. The first questions I have are very simple, have to do with our ignorance of the situation there. You told us yesterday that there was a military tribunal in Travnik, there was another one in Zenica. And my first question is: Where would the demarcation line between the two be? Where would your responsibilities end and those of the prosecutor in Zenica begin? Could you indicate where the line was?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the demarcation line depended on the territorial jurisdiction of those two courts. The Travnik was responsible for the Travnik area, and the territorial jurisdiction of the other court was for Zenica. So naturally the line of demarcation between those two municipalities was the line of demarcation for the jurisdiction of each of the courts. Sometimes this line would change. It wasn't fixed as it is now in peacetime. Sometimes the line would change. That depended on the combat operations of various units at the time. So the demarcation line -- well, for example, the combatants from the Zenica Brigade were usually dealt with by the Zenica court, whereas combatants, soldiers from Travnik or the 7th Corps, were dealt with by the Travnik court. But this was a sort of geographic line as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So there was a huge difference between territorial jurisdiction in theory or on paper and territorial jurisdiction in practice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the difference was very significant. This happened very seldom. On the whole, the territorial jurisdiction that had been established by a decree law was respected. Sometimes we would refer these cases to courts or prosecutor's offices elsewhere. We did this gladly because we had a lot of work, so we were very happy to refer cases to other courts or other prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Could you then answer me whether these places were in the territorial jurisdiction of the Travnik military court or in that of the Zenica military court or maybe even a third military court. I'm going to mention a few names of places, and if you could please indicate to what court -- what court had territorial jurisdiction over that place. The first name and I would mention is Brajkovici. Was that under your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had territorial jurisdiction over Brajkovici, because that is part of the municipality of Travnik. It's a village in the Bila area, and it was under the control of the 306th Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the place the village of Cukle? Was that yours --

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cukle too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Dusina.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Dusina was under our jurisdiction. That was the area of the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grahovcici is in the area of the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maljine is also in the area of the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehurici is also in the area of the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletici, that's in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Orasac?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a small place, though I know that area very well. But I think that is in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Judge Swart please wait for the translation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The reporting system is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've been informed that there is a problem with the system. As it was time for a break, in any case we will now have a break. But we will resume at 4.00. It's twenty to 4.00. We will have a 20-minute break, but at five to 5.00 we will have to adjourn. We'll now adjourn and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. And we will adjourn at five to 5.00 and resume again at 6.00 p.m. We will continue with the questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Witness, we were discussing the places that fell under your jurisdiction in Travnik, and I was progressing to Miletici. I did already ask you whether Miletici was under the territorial jurisdiction of the court in Travnik; is that right? Have you answered that question?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So I'll proceed now to Orasac.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Orasac was also under the court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the place or the municipality of Ovnak, is that also ...?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ovnak is on the border between the Travnik municipality and Zenica municipality. It's actually a pass, so that a part of Ovnak belongs to the territory of Travnik municipality and another part to Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So am I right in concluding that the boundary between the Travnik district and the Zenica districts is east of the River Bila? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Finally, the place of Vares. Would that be in the jurisdiction of Zenica or any other place? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't within the jurisdiction of the Travnik, and I don't know which jurisdiction it belonged to. Possibly Zenica in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were a prosecutor in a time of war. You were a military prosecutor, and you of course had to apply the criminal law of Bosnia where common offences were concerned. And I understand from what you said yesterday also that you had to apply or could apply the Chapter 16 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, where international crimes are concerned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Only it was taken over and became the law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Were there other provisions with regard to international crimes in the law of Bosnia, apart from Chapter 16?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you offhand, but I have already said, and I wish to confirm, that we were responsible for all criminal offences from the former law of the SFRY, that is, of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to that question later on. In applying Chapter 16 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, which you said became part of the law of Bosnia, were you in any way instructed by books or by courses or in other ways on the content of international humanitarian law? Did you have any solid knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We hardly had any knowledge of it, because the courts in the territory of Travnik municipality never tried those criminal offences. I must also add that most of the judges and prosecutors were beginners in law. And I can also say that it was difficult for us to get hold of the basic laws, never mind legal textbooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So that made it very difficult for you to decide whether to charge a person with a common offence or possibly with an international offence under Chapter 16.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, for me and my colleagues it wasn't difficult to make such a decision, because we really worked on the basis of our conscience and pursuant to the laws to the extent we knew them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said that you had never prosecuted any person on the basis of the provisions on international crimes because the cases simply were not there, if I reflect your words correctly as spoken yesterday. In this respect, I would like to ask you a question, on the basis of the example of the decision that has -- of the text that has been given this afternoon. The document you saw this afternoon was a case of looting a deserted Croatian house. And if I remember well, you said this is a property against the safety -- against public safety or something like that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Looting of a Croat house, like the looting of any house, was considered a theft, depending on how serious it was, whether it was aggravated theft or burglary or armed robbery, but not a threat to public safety. It was burning or the use of explosives that was considered a threat to public safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Quite right. I see in the text that it is a case of setting fire to an abandoned home of local Croats. I apologise for my mistake. But to take this example, which you considered to be an offence causing a public danger under Article 122 of the Criminal Code of Bosnia, you must have assumed, then, that it could not -- this behaviour could not constitute an international crime under the Chapter 17, then. Is that your assumption?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our assumption, and that is how we qualified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Why would you think so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this description of the act was identical with the provisions of the law. I think it was Article 304 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think it was a criminal offence envisaged by Article 304. Every burning of property was covered by this provision of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand that. But at the same time, it could be a war crime, or is that not the case?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the time period and the point of view. If now from this -- since the time has lapsed, I might consider it in that vein. But when half of Bosnia almost was burned, it would be difficult to qualify it as a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you at that time have criteria for saying destruction of abandoned Croatian houses in time of war is only an offence against public danger, or to say well, this is more than that, this is a crime under Chapter 16?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal practice in those days treated those acts as such an offence, and this applied not only to our own prosecutor's office but to most prosecutor's offices in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We had certain consultations when things were not clear in qualifying an offence or certain activities that we undertook. We would consult with the republic's prosecutor or the department of the public prosecutor's office, which was working in Zenica. Dzemaludin Mutapcic, who was an experienced prosecutor, headed that department at the time and we frequently consulted with him to clarify certain offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But -- so I'm not mistaken; you more or less spontaneously assumed that this case or cases of looting abandoned houses were common offences and not international offences. Or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We considered all those acts as being common offences, looting of abandoned houses and burning of abandoned houses as well. Though I have to say that as far as I know, there were many cases of theft of abandoned and non-abandoned houses, but there were not many cases of burning. And these two examples of a house set on fire that was shown to me yesterday and today were in the area of Dolac and Slimena, where in 1993 and after that the separation line was between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, during 1993 and after 1993. That is where the separation line was, in fact right up until the conflict between the army and the HVO ended. So that we didn't really dare to go there to carry out an on-site inspection or anything else. It is below Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yesterday there was a discussion - and this is the reason why I'm asking this - on the freedom of the court to qualify any act as the court thought fit. And you said If I get a report of the police, I will sometimes change the qualification, and on the other hand, the court may also change -- give a different qualification to the offence, to the act than I have proposed in my indictment. And there was presented an example of such a case. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My question would be in this respect: You have never seen, or have you, any verdict of the military court putting a different legal stamp on an offence in the matter of looting houses, of putting fire on houses or similar offences?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were changes of the legal qualifications of acts, but I didn't see them change anything of substance, really, in the qualifications. Though I must repeat: Our qualifications were not binding for them. There were changes of the factual state and subsequently a change of the legal qualification; however, the legal qualification in most cases remained the one that we had proposed, as it was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it never occurred that the court changed the qualification from a act against public danger into the qualification of an act under Chapter 16 of the Yugoslavian code?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you ever look at those provisions from that perspective? Did you ever study the various provisions in that chapter in order to know whether putting fire on houses by individuals or looting by individuals could amount to a crime under your law, an international crime under your law?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did study what we had, and the criminal codes we had and commentaries of criminal codes of the former SFRY. We worked on the basis of those commentaries, and that is how we qualified the offences. Let me tell you that in the practice of former courts and our own practice in the territory of the former Yugoslavia such acts did not exist. There weren't any such acts. So that in that area there wasn't any precedent really for us to rely on. We didn't have any experience with such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So for practical purposes that chapter was not relevant to your practice.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For practical purposes, there were no such cases in our previous practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I have been looking at the text of Article 142 of that chapter, which is concerned with war crimes against the civilian population. Are you familiar with the content of that provision?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with it. I really don't know which provision it is now, but certainly, we were familiar with the provisions of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I would like you to look at the text of that provision in your own language. I will give it to you by way of the court officer. And the question I would like to put to you is the following: Would you be able to tell me whether an act of violence against a person or the looting of a house or the destruction of a house or the ill-treatment of a person or even killing of a person on an individual basis by a single soldier or by a group of soldiers would be covered by Article 142 of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that is how we would qualify it, but based on the practice that we applied and on the description of the acts that we received, I think that in those days we didn't consider it to come under the provisions of Article 142 of the former Criminal Code of the SFRY or as it was taken over by Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, frankly speaking we never really used international conventions in that period nor before that. We exclusively used the national laws. And it is very difficult from this standpoint to say whether we acted properly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If I read the translation of Article 142, I read that it deals with persons who order a number of things, and it does prima facie not concern persons who simply commit offences. It seems to have regard to those who incite others or order others to do these things. Is that a correct translation of the text in your language?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And as far as I know, there wasn't a single case that would lead us to consider it to be such an act. There were no orders or instigation of people to burn or loot abandoned houses, to mistreat or beat up anyone, and especially not civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I will leave it at that for this topic at the moment. You already said that you were the head of the prosecution service in Travnik and that you had a number of staff members. So the main responsibility for investigating and prosecuting crimes was in your hands. You were the boss, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was in charge and accountable for the work of my colleagues in the department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And in that sense, in that capacity, you were the person who had to instruct military policemen, security service members, and other persons how to prosecute or how to investigate certain cases and how to make choices in their work, et cetera. Was that your daily -- part of your daily job also, to coach the police, the security service?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that I would give instructions to them, but this was also done by my colleagues, my deputies. In view of the number of employees in the prosecution service, it was really impossible for one person only to do this work; namely, depending on our duty service, the prosecutors who were on duty for one-third of the month were also in charge of cooperation with units and persons who were responsible for the discovery of perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, in dealing with the people in the field, so to speak, who have to do the investigative work, did you -- or could you perhaps, I should ask, did you set priorities to them? Did you, for instance, say, "Well, concentrate yourself on that type of cases or -- and not on other types of cases." Or were you passive in this field?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did set priorities, and we had the greatest interest for serious crimes, particularly murder and robbery. Of course for theft and everything else, that was a daily occurrence; we didn't have too much time. So our priority were the more serious criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you received reports mainly from three units under your jurisdiction, the 302nd Brigade, the -- no, the 306th Brigade, the 307th Brigade, and the 17th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 312th and 317th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: 312th also? Because that is missing from the transcript. Were there other units you got cases from? Do you still recall which units they were?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the actual numbers by which they were known, but for the whole area that we covered - and especially from Bugojno there were a large number of criminal reports, from Novi Travnik, from Kiseljak, Fojnica - I think from all these areas we received criminal reports, and that is why, as I already said, we organised investigations in Bugojno as well and we even carried out trials. We took a part of the hotel for our investigations and trials to make it more effective and speedier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Given the mass of cases that you must have had in those years, my colleague has already put a question in that direction. Did you have regular meetings with the commanders of these units who were responsible for the crimes that the military police discovered, for dealing with these crimes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were always in contact with them, and I think that cooperation was quite satisfactory. They really followed up on our instructions, carried out our orders. They did everything they could at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did they have their own powers and military law to do investigations?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't carry out investigations, but they gathered the necessary information and evidence, but it was the investigating judge who conducted the investigations. In fact, they were most active before a report was filed and from the time a report was filed up until the time the case was referred to the court or, rather, to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said that you acted on reports of victims, reports of the police, reports of the security services, that in some situations you referred the case to the investigating judge; in other cases you took your own initiative within the framework of the criminal procedure. My question is: Did you ever take any initiative without a report or without a complaint by a specific victim or through a family member?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, sometimes we did take certain measures if we knew that something had happened. But we had limited access to information. It was limited to the core area of Travnik. Our movement was restricted. It took place within a radius of a few kilometres. The other areas were areas where the various parties in the conflict were fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I don't understand -- quite understand your last remark. What do you mean by saying that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that according to the law it was our duty to take action if we found out about crimes that had been committed. This is also what the law states in Bosnia and Herzegovina at present. I don't know whether any other law enforcement agencies took action with regard to such crimes, but we could take certain action before proceedings were instituted in order to gather evidence that related to what we knew about. But we had very limited knowledge at that time, because we lived and worked in incredible conditions, in very difficult conditions. Movement restricted to the core area of the town. It's not because someone had imposed these restrictions upon us, but it's because the town was shelled almost on a daily basis, that there were lines above Travnik, 8 kilometres above Travnik and 2 kilometres below Travnik, so that this should tell you how restricted our movement was. Even in the areas that you have mentioned, we sometimes went to those areas and conducted investigations. That depended on the crimes that had been reported. But going into such areas was extremely dangerous. One risked one's life because there was fighting in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to interrupt you here because I was -- I had in mind to ask you something different. But now that you have said this, you were restricted in your movements and limited practically speaking to Travnik and the immediate surroundings, that would not be valid for your -- for the military police or the security service who were part of the army, I suppose? They were much freer in moving over the area they controlled. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally it depended on the situation at the time, but they could move around the entire area that was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you communicate with them by telephone or by radio or by whatever else you had without physically meeting each other?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We communicated by telephone, but only with the brigade command -- or rather, with the place where they were deployed, and that was in the area of Travnik, in Bugojno, or with the brigades outside of Travnik. We didn't have any contact with certain brigades, apart from contact via courier -- or rather, we didn't have any direct contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What I had in mind to ask you is the following: You acted on reports of the army, of the military police, of security service. You acted upon the reports of people who came to tell you that they were victims. You said also -- you implied that you had other sources of information to act upon.
