My question is: In the situation of Bosnia in 1993, did you also act on the basis of rumours or of messages in the press or in -- on the stories of journalists or international reporters, radio, television, which are not official channels of communication for you, of course; but ...?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could take such action, but I must say that this happened rarely, and the scope of the action was limited. The media was almost non-existent. We didn't even have electricity, let alone newspapers and magazines. There were very few lucky people who had electricity and were able to listen to the radio, so you must realise the situation we were in. And the information that we did receive was mostly censored. As you are well aware, in wartime conditions censorship is applied everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I see I am too optimistic about your possibilities of hearing -- receiving information from a number of sources. Did you ever meet any international official in your capacity as a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, during the war we almost never met international representatives, international officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. My final question has regard to what you said yesterday about prosecuting a number of offences. I have to look where I have it. You said about burning Croat houses: "As far as I remember, there has been no case in which there has been a prosecution." Today you were shown a document which makes it likely that there was at least one case in which you prosecuted the author of such an offence. As far as war crimes are concerned or crimes against humanity, you said yesterday, "As far as I can recall, I got no reports from anyone." And as far as ill-treatment of prisoners is concerned, you said: "With regard to civilian prisoners, as far as I can recollect, I never received reports." I'm now quoting from the transcript of yesterday. My question is more or less: If you used such expressions "as far as I can recall," "as far as I can remember," "as far as I can recollect," what content would you give these statements? They are in a way rather vague. It may mean 60 per cent. It may mean 90 per cent certain. Could you specify a little bit what you mean by "as far as I can recall."

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to tell you what the percentage would be, but I think it would be above 90 per cent. I think that my memory is correct 90 per cent of the time. Perhaps I have forgotten certain things, but when houses were torched, well, I characterised this as other crimes. It was only when I was given the case that I realised that it was a case of houses being torched, because at that time and even today if a building is torched, this represents a threat to public safety, according to our law. So I focussed on another aspect of the case. But as far as the other cases I have mentioned, over 90 per cent of what I said is certainly correct. So that is the extent to which my memory would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. You have, I suppose - but correct me if I'm wrong - before you came here had an interview with a researcher or a member of the Prosecution team of the Tribunal. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was it a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a meeting in Sarajevo last year, in the autumn of last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think it was in November. I also had a meeting with representatives of the Prosecution immediately prior to giving my testimony; that is to say, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And that was the first time, I suppose, that you meet any representative of the Prosecutors of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed last November last year, before being interviewed had you performed a check on your files, if they still existed, or were there any other means for you of checking your memory?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't check them, and I have no intention of checking them any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How do you mean "I have no intention of checking them any more"? If you would be asked to do it now, you would refuse? Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have so many other obligations. I would prefer it if I could just forget that entire period. There were many things that happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few more questions. Did you do your military service in the JNA, in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you were appointed as military prosecutor, what did you do in the month before you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the municipality of Travnik. At the time, since we had parallel bodies at the time - the BH army and the HVO were these parallel bodies - so I was practically appointed as the Secretary for National Defence. That took place a few months before I was appointed; that is to say, a few months before I went to the military district prosecutor's office. In peacetime, I worked for the same body, but I was the second man, so to speak. There was the secretary, and I was the sort of manager for the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As military prosecutor, did you wear civilian clothes or were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wore civilian clothes at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military court, in relation to the -- how far was it from the ex-JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military court and the military prosecutor's office were in the premises of the court which exists in Travnik today. That's about a distance of 2 to 3 hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the time, your office and the JNA barracks, how far was your office from the barracks? We're talking about the period of May to December 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same distance as today, 2 or 3 hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The text that you drafted at the time gave you a lot of power, in accordance with Article 5 signed by President Izetbegovic, the power to launch investigations when crimes were committed or when there were offences. As part of this mission, were you concerned with the detention facilities managed by the army? Did you deal with these facilities?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as detention facilities that the army ran are concerned, this was the responsibility of the court. We had a military detention facility, and the president of the court had the responsibility to take care of the detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For you, the army's detention facility was located where exactly in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army's detention facility was in the building of the former railway administration building. It's in the immediate vicinity of the court and the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, there were no other detention facilities. That was the only official detention facility. Or were there others too?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the barracks in Travnik, there was a detention unit, but it was for disciplinary purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As a military prosecutor, did you as prosecutor also have any responsibilities with regard to public and individual liberties? Was it part of your obligations to go and visit these detention facilities to see what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all times, at any time I could go and visit those detention facilities if I wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you in the former JNA barracks? Did you visit the former JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you meet any of the detainees there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these members of the military -- members of the military and civilians, or civilians?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you speak to them?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you check to see whether they were legally detained there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They all had the appropriate decisions on detention. None of them had been detained without there being an order issued by the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you can remember, when examining the texts that deal with the liberty or detention of persons under the control of the army, it would appear that after two hours of detention it was necessary to inform the judicial or military authority of this. There were rules governing detention. Were these rules respected by the army?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about the practice at the time. The officer -- each officer of every unit, of brigades, of corps, could issue a decision on disciplinary detention for 15 or 30 days. So such was the practice. These soldiers would be detained for 15 or, rather, for 30 days when disciplinary measures were taken against them. And during that period of time, we could carry out other investigations in order to support the detention or justify the detention of the person concerned. So everything was done in accordance with the rules in force. Unless -- but this wasn't the case for people who weren't members of those units -- or rather, if there were people from some other army present in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. In such cases we would issue urgent decisions on detention, because the officer then had no right to decide on imposing disciplinary detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the BH army detained a HVO soldier, the fact that the HVO soldier was detained by the army, would that automatically mean that you would be informed of this?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the detention facilities I have mentioned, the ones I was familiar with, we were immediately informed of such cases in the case of these detention facilities. As to whether there were any other cases, I don't know. But as far as I do know, I don't think there were any other such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling me that if an HVO soldier had been imprisoned, you should have been informed of the fact that this soldier had been taken into detention. That is what you're telling us, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They should have provided us with a report and on that basis we would suggest that the court issue a decision on detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My very last question, since we have to make the break: There were a number of military prosecutors in various areas. You were the prosecutor in Travnik. Did you and your colleagues, the other military prosecutors, have meetings? If you didn't have meetings, did you speak to each other over the phone to inform each other of what you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had meetings with prosecutors from Zenica. Everything else was under blockade and we had no contact whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And above you - because a prosecutor always has a superior. It's just as it is in the army; you always have a superior - who was your superior? Who was your military superior?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My military superior? I didn't have a military superior. But I did have a superior in the prosecution. The prosecutor above me was the deputy of the republican prosecutor, who had a branch office in Zenica, the civilian republic prosecutor. Dzemaludin Mutapcic was his name. I mentioned his name a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So he was your superior.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have to have a break now. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as not to waste any time, I have just one question to put to the witness. Have the Defence any additional questions and about how long would they take?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes, not more. Maybe even less. I have three topics which I should like to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So ten minutes. And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Probably none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And is it other witness ready to start? Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the next witness is ready to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't understand why we're wasting time. The witness should have been here. We knew that we would resume at 6.00 p.m., and he should have been here. We will make sure that we don't waste time in the future in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to inform the Chamber that we are now in a position to inform the Prosecution of the number of documents and specifically which documents coming from the European Union Monitoring Mission that we are ready to inform the Prosecution about already today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one last question to put to you before giving you to the Defence. In your position as military prosecutor, when you received information or when you had investigations conducted, but prior to the judges, was the military police the institution which had to respond to your instructions or to comply with your instructions?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Travnik, what was the name of the person in charge of the military police who was the person you communicated with for that sort of problem, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know what his name was. I know that he wasn't from Travnik but from the Bosnian Krajina. I really can't remember his name, because he wasn't a local and that's why I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that you would see him, call him up on the phone, you would meet with him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zeric, I have a couple of questions for you connected to the questions you were asked by Their Honours. You were asked several questions relative to the burning of houses and the qualification of those acts. I am quite sure that you're well aware that during combat operations and immediately after them the village of Bandol was totally destroyed and burnt down by the HVO. Is this a fact you were aware of in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. One of my associates, actually an assistant, an administrative clerk, came from the environs of that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Zeric, that you never saw nor learnt about any event when the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina captured a village which had previously been inhabited by Croats? You never learnt of the army totally destroying or burning down a village?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any such information that any village in the territory of Travnik municipality or beyond it with a majority Croat population, which they had abandoned, had been totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all the reported acts, thefts, robberies, burning of houses, you received those reports after the combat operations as individual acts committed by individual civilians or military persons?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were individual cases after combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that also one of the reasons why you never -- it never occurred to you to qualify those acts in any other way but the way envisaged by our laws?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As regards another question put to you by the Presiding Judge, I would like to clarify a few things with you, namely: In answer to a question from the Presiding Judge, you said that military authorities could put a soldier in detention up to 30 days as a disciplinary measure and this detention could be extended by a decision of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said if a member of the HVO were to be detained, then the investigating judge would determine the detention.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only the investigating judge had that right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this occurred in situations when there were grounds to suspect that those persons had committed a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that if the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina during combat operations had captured an enemy soldier simply as a prisoner of war, then you as the prosecutors and the court had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We had no contact with such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A third issue that I would like you to confirm for me is that Her Honour the Judge, asked you a question about this and I want to check whether I'm right if I say the following: Would you agree with me if I say that the Mujahedin in 1993 were not members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that as a result the military police had no authority to investigate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Objection. Outside of the witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You only started the sentence and Mr. Stamp got up. What is the problem, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's not a problem. It's an objection. She's asking the witness whether or not he knows whether certain people were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He, on the basis of his testimony so far, is not competent to give evidence as to who were or who were not members of the army. It's not within his area of competence. He might speculate. And if - and I would submit that the Court ought not to be accepting or eliciting - I would submit that the Court ought not to be allowing questions that seek to elicit speculation. That is the objection. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the question was put to the military prosecutor at the time. In view of his position as military prosecutor he should have some considerable knowledge of the jurisdiction over which he had powers. And as he had military personnel under his control and to ask him whether he knew - but he can tell us, he knew or did not - whether among the military people over whom he had control there were any Mujahedin. That is the gist of your question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Her Honour asked a question about Mujahedin, and proceeding on the basis that you suggested I wanted to ask this witness that question. I can also rephrase it and say: Is it right that the Mujahedin or the foreign fighters that appeared in the area of Travnik, that they were not in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that what you -- your knowledge from that time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The objection is the same. And I respectfully ask that there be a ruling whether or not this witness is competent to testify about who were members of the army. He may be competent to testify about what was reported to him in respect to the charges. He might be competent to testify about investigation, but he's not competent to testify about who were or who were not at any particular time officially or not officially personnel of the ABiH. He'd be speculating, it is my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In view of the question put and the objection made, and in view of the fact that a Judge asked a question about the Mujahedin, the Chamber is going to ask the witness to tell us: Within his jurisdiction in territorial terms Travnik and the surroundings of Travnik, on the basis of the reports you had, the knowledge you had at a given moment in time, did you know that there were among the BH army members elements which could be called Mujahedin? You knew that or you didn't know that. The question is a very simple one, especially in view of the position that you held. If you were just a farmer, of course the question would not be put to you. But you are not a simple farmer. You were an important person in the life of the community, and therefore you may be able to answer this question. But if you don't know, tell me frankly. I must remind you that you took a solemn oath to tell us the whole truth, and your answer must reflect that, must be the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the organisation of the army is concerned and who comprised the various units, who were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I really did not have detailed information about that. But on the basis of other circumstances and the overall activities in the area, I know that there were no reports against foreign fighters and Mujahedin, though I do know that they did commit some criminal offences in the town itself. However, we had in reality no jurisdiction over them. I was an eyewitness of an event when I could have easily got killed in a coffee bar I was sitting in. A Mujahedin walked in and opened fire arbitrarily at us and the facility but we couldn't arrest him nor could we take any steps against him. Nor was I able to order anyone from the military to undertake such steps. I believe that you will be able to understand the substance of what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, you have answered a part of my question, but I'm asking you now -- I have two more questions, actually. Is it true that after combat operations in certain areas the civilian police would take over the duty to take care of the safety and security of persons and property?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the duty of the civilian police, to protect people and property who were outside combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the military police, if it were to learn that certain persons - be they nationals or foreigners who were not members of the army - had committed a crime, then it was the civilian police's duty to investigate that and report it to the public prosecutor and not to you as the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian police was responsible for all the civilians and everything they did in a given area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even when those persons were in military uniform and carried weapons, as you told us, who opened fire at you in fact, if they were not members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. 90 per cent of the population in those days wore some sort of uniform. But in order to show whether somebody was a member of the army or not, he had to have an official ID, and those persons would be searched for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zeric. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My colleague tells me that on page 58, line 6 it was stated in French "the military police," but instead it should read "the civilian police." I have to check myself what it is the witness said. In the transcript, it is stated correctly that it was now the duty of the civilian police, but my colleague informs me that in French it was stated "the military police" instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stamp, no questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Well, sir, we thank you. You have been testifying for two days. I can imagine that this required an effort on your part to jog your memory in order to be able to answer our questions. Thank you for your contribution to the establishment of the truth. We wish you a safe journey home, and best wishes in exercising your current duties as prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have another 40 minutes, we will bring the witness in. We can ask him to take the solemn declaration, and we can start with his testimony. Mr. Withopf, in the written document regarding the duration of the examination-in-chief, I think that you envisaged two hours. Will your examination-in-chief indeed take two hours for this witness? We will now have about 40 minutes, but we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, yours -- Your Honours, indeed I anticipate the examination-in-chief lasting for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In those circumstances, tomorrow after the examination-in-chief we can address the question of documents that would have been schedule for Thursday. Mr. Bourgon explained to us a moment ago that the matter is about to be resolved with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed all the lists have been provided to us by the Prosecution. We have now completed our work. We are going to give them back the CDs with the numbers of the documents that we haven't received and that are in the possession of the Prosecution. It is now up to the Prosecution to get permission for disclosing them to us, and that will be done as quickly as possible, and then we will be able to proceed with the European Monitoring Mission witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Bourgon. Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while waiting for the witness, I should like to inform the Trial Chamber that tomorrow and the day after the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic will be represented by my colleague Mr. Bourgon and the legal assistants, and in accordance with my client I will not be present in the courtroom, and I wish to inform the Trial Chamber about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and within the framework of your testimony I need to have your identification, so please will tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Martin Garrod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date and place of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 29th of May, 1935 in a place called Darjeeling in India.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm retired at the moment. My career was in the military in the Royal Marines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your position at the time and within what framework did you exercise that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, I came out to Bosnia as a member of the EC Monitor Mission, first of all going to Mostar in the summer of 1993 just after the war between the Croats and the Bosniaks had started, and then in October I moved up to Zenica, which was the headquarters of the monitor mission in Bosnia as the head of the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you had a position on behalf of the European Community. But before that, were you active in your own country? Did you have a military position or rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I served for 37 years in the Royal Marines, ending up as the head of the Royal Marines in the rank of lieutenant general; in other words, a three star.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is this the first time for you to testify in an international tribunal, or have you already testified in a national court about the facts that occurred in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my third attendance here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you recollect in which cases you testified before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, Dario Kordic; and then secondly, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Will you please read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated. As you already have some experience as a witness, my information will be brief. As you know, you have been called by the Prosecution to testify about the facts of which you were a witness, an eyewitness, and it is for that reason that the Prosecution has asked you to come. You will therefore be answering questions put to you by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. Following those questions by representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right, you will be answering questions put to you by the representatives of the accused, who are on your left. There are now four; usually there are six, but only two of them will have questions for you. And tomorrow, in fact, there will only be three, because one of them will be absent. So you will be answering questions within the framework of the cross-examination. Also, the three Judges in front of you may, as provided for by the Rules which govern the work of this Tribunal, ask you questions. It is slightly different from the common-law system because we, too, are allowed to put questions to you because this system is a kind of hybrid between the common- and civil-law systems. And the Judges will be asking you questions either to clarify certain answers that you may have made or because they feel that there are certain shortcomings in your answers, certain things that need to be filled in, as this is primarily an oral proceedings of an adversarial type. Try to answer the questions to the best of your ability, of course. If you don't remember a particular fact, you will tell us so, because sometimes it is indeed very difficult to remember what took place ten years ago. Also, two minor additional points: You have taken the solemn oath to tell us the whole truth, which of course excludes false testimony. As you know, false testimony can be prosecuted by a fine or a prison term. And a second point that I need to make is that should a witness in answering questions provide certain incriminating elements, he need not answer them. The Court may compel the witness to answer, but in that case he enjoys a kind of immunity. That is how your testimony will proceed. Today we will have about half an hour, but we will continue tomorrow. Unfortunately, you will be asked to come back again later because the Defence didn't have the necessary documents in their possession and they need to study them before they are able to properly conduct their cross-examination; therefore, we will ask you kindly to come back probably sometime in May. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir Martin. Sir Martin, you already informed the Trial Chamber that you after 37 years -- after serving a 37 years' career within the British Army you retired as a three-star general. Would it be fair to say that prior to your retirement you were the overall senior officer in charge of the entire British Marine force, the British Royal Marines?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it also be fair to say, Sir Martin, without going into any further detail, that over the years you served in a number of positions and in a number of ranks and, of course, in a number of different locations, including overseas?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you already informed the Trial Chamber that you became a member of the ECMM. Can you please tell us as to when you became a member of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I came out to Bosnia, well, via Zagreb, in the late June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what the abbreviation ECMM stands for.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It stands for the EC - European Community - Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In late June 1993, Sir Martin, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I first of all went to Zenica, which is right in the middle of Central Bosnia, which was the headquarters, known as the regional centre, of all the EC monitors in Bosnia. I went there for initial briefing along with several other newly joined monitors who were going to Bosnia, and I was there for about ten days to a fortnight being briefed, having -- and getting to know the area and getting to know -- getting a feel for the problems that existed in Bosnia. After that, I was then sent down to Mostar to take over as the head of the coordinating centre based in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir Martin, for how long have you been the head of the coordinating centre based in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I -- from very early July until mid-October, when I was reappointed to Zenica to take over as the head of the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for how long, Sir Martin, have you been the head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: For almost exactly six months, from mid-October to mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mid-April --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Mid-April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well, Sir Martin. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber who was your predecessor as the head of the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. It was a French diplomat, Jean-Pierre Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prior to taking over your position as the head of the regional centre in Zenica, did you have an opportunity to talk to Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, we talked quite a lot during my initial ten days or a fortnight in Zenica. And then while I was down in Mostar we were in regular touch; and Jean-Pierre Thebault used to come down to visit me in Mostar and I would go up to Zenica for meetings. So we were in regular touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were already saying, Sir Martin, that you got briefings about the situation in Central Bosnia already in June but later on in the course of meetings and conversations with Ambassador Thebault. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what sort of issues have been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, we discussed the key issues on which the EC monitors reported in the priority of political matters, military matters, and humanitarian matters, and then any other matters of interest. But those were the three key topics on which we concentrated for our monitoring and for our reporting. I should add that of course in Bosnia it, as very often happened, that the political and the military were very closely interlinked, and so one could talk to political leaders about military matters and military leaders about political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Prior to going into any further detail in relation to what you just stated, Sir Martin, can you please inform the Trial Chamber in some detail about the mission and the mandate of the ECMM in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Would you like me to outline the organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The organisation, its structures, but also its mandate.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The EC Monitor Mission was deployed throughout the former Yugoslavia. But if I could concentrate on Bosnia. At the top, one had the regional centre, which, as I have mentioned, was based in Zenica, right in the centre. The regional centre would have under it a number of coordinating centres, and in Bosnia there were three: Tuzla in the north, Travnik in the centre, and Mostar in the south. And each of those coordinating centres would be led by the head of the coordinating centre, the HCC. In each coordinating centre, there would be a number of monitor teams. For instance, in Mostar and in Central Bosnia, in Travnik, they each had four teams, four teams; and in Tuzla, there were three teams. Each team consisted of two international monitors of different nationalities together with a driver and an interpreter. And they were really the workhorses who went out and did the basic work on the ground, providing the information for our reporting system. And the reporting system was that the two-man monitor teams at the end of the day would provide a written report which would be transmitted to their coordinating centre. The head of the coordinating centre would then amalgamate those team reports into a consolidated report and send that to the regional centre. And the regional centre would then coordinate the three coordinating centre reports and provide a regional centre report, which would be dispatched to the headquarters of the ECMM, which at that stage was in Zagreb. They in their turn would provide an overall report, including those from the various different regional centres, which would go off to the various capitals of the EC or EU, so that each foreign ministry would have a report during the night or on their desks first thing in the morning giving them hopefully a comprehensive review of the state of political matters, military matters, humanitarian matters in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir Martin, may I please in following up what you just said ask you a few further questions. As the head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica, what was your area of responsibility, the geographical area, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It was a large area, extending from Tuzla in the north down through Central Bosnia, down to Mostar in the south. And, in fact, it covered all areas of Bosnia except for the areas which was known then as Republika Srpska, which was the Serb-occupied areas of Bosnia, and the pockets. By "pockets" I mean the little islands of Bosniak territory in a Serb sea, and those pockets were Sarajevo; the Bihac pocket, on the west, and the small enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The main area in which I was concerned was a triangle which went up from the south up round the top, over Tuzla, and then down, running close to Mostar, just to the west of Mostar, and then on down to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were informing the Trial Chamber, Sir Martin, that you had three coordination centres under your command and one of them was the coordination centre in Travnik. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what was the area of responsibility, the geographical area, of the coordination centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Again, the coordination centre in Travnik had a large area to cover with his four two-man teams. This extended from Zavidovici and -- up in the north and Vares in the north, down through Travnik in Central Bosnia and down to Bugojno -- Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us, Sir Martin, who -- during the time you were the head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica, who was your deputy and who was working in the coordination centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. My -- my deputy was a -- happened to be another former British former army officer called Geoff Beaumont. The operations officer was a Dane called Aage Terp. And the head of the coordinating centre in Travnik was a Canadian lieutenant colonel called William Stutt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already touched a bit on the following issue. Can you please in some more detail inform us on how information was collected on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The information was collected by the monitoring teams, also by the heads of the coordinating centres, and also by the head of the regional centre, because we also all went out ourselves and had meetings and found out things. The monitors on the ground would make contact with military leaders, civil leaders, international people in their area to gather as much information on what was going on, as I say, in the political field, the military field, and humanitarian field in that order. The extent of how successful they were and the quality of the information that they provided depended very much on the calibre of the monitors themselves. Some were outstanding, but there were one or two who were not quite so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the time you've been the head of the regional centre in Zenica, how would you describe the ones who worked for you in the coordination centre in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, as I say, the ones who didn't come up to scratch were very, very few and far between. I was very satisfied overall with the standard of the monitors that we had throughout the whole regional centre, and indeed, the monitors in the coordinating centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you already touched on the issue of the reporting system. I understand there were daily reports sent, if I recall correctly. You said it earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The daily reports? Yes. As I say, the monitors on the ground would send up their reports to the coordinating centres. The coordinating centres would send them up to the regional centre. And the regional centre would then coordinate the full report which would go off to the headquarters of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the purpose of such reports?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The purpose of the reports was to enable the various nations, and in particular their foreign ministries, to be fully informed of the situation on the ground in the various countries of the former Yugoslavia so that they could keep right up to date with the -- our assessment of the political situation, the military situation, and the humanitarian situation, and any other points of significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please briefly detail your own involvement in drafting and sending such reports.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the nightly report that was sent off from the regional centre was initially compiled by my deputy and by the operations officer. They would get the reports together, produce a consolidated report, and then that would come to me. I would then -- I might query one or two of the things in it, but if I was satisfied, then I might add my own comments at the end, which would go under a separate paragraph called "HRC's comments." And then that would be dispatched to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Sir Martin, you basically did get to know about the contents of all such reports, even if you did not yourself draft the reports.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I may not have read -- I may not have been able to read all the coordinating centre reports in detail, which would then be included into the regional centre report, but if there was anything there in which I wanted more detail, then I would go to the full coordinating centre report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you, Sir Martin, did you have to give your approval prior to sending the reports?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I would give my approval, and then it would be sent. I would also produce my own reports, so-called special reports, on particular items of interest or any particular important meetings that I attended myself. And also on a weekly basis I would give what we called the HRC's assessment of the situation, assessing points of significance and trying to forecast what might happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: From what you just told us, Sir Martin, would the conclusion be fair -- would it be fair to say that you are in a position to comment on ECMM reports even if you have not drafted them yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Sir Martin, let's move on to a different item. Which military or which armies were active in the area of Central Bosnia during the time you've been the head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, it was fundamentally a war between the Croats and the Bosniaks within my area of responsibility. Of course, the Serbs were to either side just outside my area of responsibility, but in my area of responsibility it was a war between the Croats and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On the Bosniak side, which corps was responsible for fighting this war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, it was 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And on the opposite side, on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It was the HVO -- they used to call it the operational zone of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How would you, Sir Martin, describe in some detail the military situation within the ABiH 3rd Corps at the time you arrived in Zenica and later on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, the fighting was fierce. There were a number of Croat pockets in the area, in particular, Vares in the north, Kiseljak in the south, and in the centre, Vitez and Busovaca. I always assessed that the aims of both sides was to seize territory, bearing in mind they must have known that when a cease-fire eventually came the possession of territory is nine-tenths of the law, and what has actually been seized by armies in war is difficult to claw back under a peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Which army, from what you got to know, Sir Martin, which army was the, if I may use plain language, was the strong army at the time in October 1993 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, there are different ways of assessing strength. One can assess it in terms of numbers or in terms of weaponry. Now, the arms embargo placed on the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia, of course which they objected to very strongly, blaming in particular the British and the French, because the Bosniaks said this was very unfair on them because the Serbs had Serbia on their border and the Croats had Croatia, and therefore the Serbs and the Croats could obtain weapons and ammunition and arms across the border from their - for want of a better word - parent countries; whereas the Bosniaks were not able to do so because they were locked in on all sides. But -- so I would say that from the point of view of weapons, the Serbs and the Croats had the big advantage. But the Bosniaks' advantage was the manpower; they had a larger number of men that they could call on and were slowly building up the size of their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just informing the Trial Chamber, Sir Martin, that the manpower of the ABiH was significantly larger than on the HVO side. Was it twice as much, three times as much? How much larger was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't have the exact figures in my head, but from memory I would say that the Bosniak manpower population was well over twice that of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this also apply for the situation within the area of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I would say maybe in the 3rd Corps it might have even been higher, because it was -- by then a large number of the Croats had moved down to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you, Sir Martin, did you become aware of refugees, Muslim refugees from other areas coming to the area of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. There were many refugees, and in fact in Zenica in particular, again off the top of my head, I think from a population in Zenica of some 200.000 at least 50.000 were displaced people from elsewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you would just allow me to finish this line of questioning. It will certainly not take me longer than three to four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Among these refugees coming into the area of the 3rd Corps, were there men in a military age?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, there would have been men of a military age. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Sir Martin, what was considered being of a military age?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I'd say it was 16 or 17 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, Sir Martin - and this would be my last question for today - were refugees, Muslim refugees of a military age which came to the area of the ABiH 3rd Corps, were they incorporated into this 3rd Corps, into military units subordinated to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: To my knowledge, all men of military age were called up into the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would suggest to for today to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. It's now 7.00, and for technical reasons we have to adjourn. We will stop at 7.00 today. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00. Sir Garrod, we will see you tomorrow morning at 9.00. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no other issues to raise - I'll give the floor to Mr. Bourgon - tomorrow we'll continue with the examination-in-chief of this witness, and we will then have two other stages to follow. We will tender documents that are not being contested by the Defence. These documents will be given official exhibit numbers tomorrow when we are provided with the eight binders by the Prosecution. Tomorrow we'll have the 92 bis statements. They haven't yet been given any numbers. And on the basis of a list of statements, we will give these written statements, the 92 bis statements, exhibit numbers. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was just something I wanted to point out. That since the beginning of this testimony we have been saying "Sir Martin," I think that Martin is the witness's first name. I just wanted to point this out, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, I think that his family name is Garrod, and Martin must be his first name. But perhaps he has both names. I don't know. Perhaps the Prosecution could enlighten us. Perhaps he has a double-barrelled name. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not want to go in too much detail about the customs how a person who has been given the "Sir" by the British Queen has to be addressed. If my learned friends from the Defence side and the Trial Chamber would consult -- it's custom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That wasn't Mr. Bourgon's question. Mr. Bourgon was wondering whether his name was Martin or Garrod, whether his first name was Martin or Garrod. What is his first name? Is Martin the first name or not? That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleague has told me that Sir Martin is quite appropriate, so we stand corrected, and I apologise to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We don't have problems of any kind. We just needed to clarify this matter. Mr. Dixon, thank you for helping us resolve this semantic issue. I would like to thank all the parties, and I invite you to return tomorrow for the hearing that will start at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
